Term Insurance

Pure life cover for your family · regulated by IRDAI

Term insurance keeps your family’s plans on track if you are not there to provide for them. You pay a premium, yearly or monthly. If something happens to you during the policy term, your family receives the full cover amount (the sum assured).

How to recognise it

  • It replaces your income for your family, so loans, school fees and monthly expenses stay covered.
  • The premium is fixed when you buy, and usually stays the same for the whole term.
  • Your family can receive the money in one go, as a monthly income, or both. You choose when you buy.

Often confused with

Endowment and money-back plans. They combine savings with cover. Already have one? Talk to us before you stop it.

Health insurance. Pays hospital bills; term insurance does not (entry 02).

3Facts as of October 2026
01 · Term insuranceProtect
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
IRDAI, the insurance regulator.
What you pay
A premium, paid yearly or monthly, fixed when you buy. It depends on your age, health, habits such as smoking, the cover amount and the term.
Time commitment
The term you choose, usually until your earning years end (age 60 to 70). You have 30 days to return a new policy if it does not suit you (free look).
When it pays
To your family (your nominee) if something happens to you during the term. Subject to policy terms, the insurer must pay within 15 days of getting all papers, or 45 days if it needs to check the claim.
Costs
Only the premium. No GST on individual policies since 22 September 2025.
Tax in brief
Old tax regime only: claim the premium under Section 123 (earlier 80C), within its ₹1.5 lakh yearly limit. The money your family receives is tax-free.

Work out your coverRule of thumb: 10 to 15 times yearly income

AYearly household expenses₹
D+ Loans still to repay₹
B× Years your family needs support
E+ Big goals: education, marriage₹
C= Income to replace (A × B)₹
F− Savings and existing cover₹
Cover you need = C + D + E − F₹

Use it for

  • Replacing your income for your family
  • Clearing a home loan in your absence
  • Your children’s education, whatever happens

How we help

  • Work out the cover your family needs
  • Compare plans and claim records
  • Stand by your family at claim time

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • Is the cover enough for my family’s plans, including my loans?
  • Have I shared every health detail, habit and existing policy?
  • Who is my nominee, and does my family know about this policy?

Health Insurance

Hospital cover for your family · regulated by IRDAI

You pay a premium every year. If you need hospital treatment, the insurer pays the bills up to your sum insured. It pays the hospital directly (cashless) or pays you back, so you can focus on getting well, not on the bill.

How to recognise it

  • It pays actual hospital bills up to the sum insured, for one person or for the whole family on one policy (floater).
  • A claim-free year can raise your cover (no-claim bonus). Some policies refill cover you have used up during the year (restoration).
  • You can move to another insurer and keep credit for the waiting time you have already served (portability).

Often confused with

Critical illness cover. Pays a fixed lump sum when a listed illness is diagnosed, whatever the bill. Use it alongside health insurance.

Employer cover. Usually ends when you change jobs or retire.

Mutual Funds

Pooled, professionally managed · regulated by SEBI

Many investors put their money into one pool. A professional fund manager invests it in shares, bonds, gold or other assets, as the scheme’s rules allow. You own units of the pool. The price of one unit (the NAV) is published every business day.

How to recognise it

  • You own units of a pool, not the shares or bonds themselves.
  • Every scheme has a Direct and a Regular plan. A Regular plan, bought through a distributor like us, includes our commission for our service.
  • Each scheme must stick to its label. For example, a large-cap fund keeps at least 80% in large companies.

Often confused with

SIF. Same fund houses and tax rules, with tools for rising, falling and sideways markets. Entry 04, next.

ULIP. An insurance policy with an investment part, regulated by IRDAI. It is not a mutual fund.

SIF

Specialised investment funds · regulated by SEBI

A SIF is run by a mutual fund house under SEBI’s mutual fund rules, and is taxed like a mutual fund. Its manager has more tools: it can gain when prices fall, move between asset types, and turn market exposure up or down.

How to recognise it

  • Has tools for rising, falling and sideways markets: the manager can raise or cut exposure, and take short positions with up to 25% of the fund.
  • Taxed like a mutual fund: nothing is taxed inside the fund. In the growth option, you pay tax only when you redeem or switch.
  • Can be cautious or adventurous. Each strategy’s Risk Band, from Level 1 (lowest risk) to Level 5 (highest), tells you which.

Often confused with

Mutual funds. Same fund houses, tax rules and safeguards. A SIF adds tools for falling and sideways markets, and starts at ₹10 lakh.

Category III AIFs and PMS. Similar tools (fewer in a PMS), but taxed every year. In a SIF, tax waits until you redeem or switch.

10Ram Investments · Diary 2027
Pages 11–12
BuildKnow your products · 04 in depth

SIF in depth

What a SIF manager can do

Fund houses explain SIFs with simple examples like these. Each shows one tool a SIF can use that an equity mutual fund cannot, or can use only in part.

Markets fall

Protect the portfolio

  1. What happensA sudden shock threatens to pull the whole market down.
  2. What the manager doesSells index futures against part of the fund. This is a hedge.
  3. What can followIf the market falls, the hedge gains and offsets part of the loss. If it does not, the hedge costs a little.

One weak company

Gain from its fall

  1. What happensA company looks overpriced, and its business is weakening.
  2. What the manager doesTakes a short position in its futures, for a small part of the fund.
  3. What can followIf the price falls, the fund gains. If it rises, that position loses. An equity mutual fund cannot do this.

Markets go sideways

Earn a price gap

  1. What happensA share and its one-month future trade at slightly different prices.
  2. What the manager doesBuys the share and sells the future together. This is arbitrage.
  3. What can followAt expiry the two prices meet, so the gap is earned whether the share rises, stays or falls, less costs.

Hypothetical examples, to show how the tools work. Real strategies differ, and the manager’s calls can be wrong.

NCDs

Non-convertible debentures · regulated by SEBI

An NCD is a loan you give a company for a fixed period. The company pays you interest at a fixed rate and returns your money at the end (maturity). It can never be turned into shares, so it is called “non-convertible”.

How to recognise it

  • Fixed interest, paid monthly, yearly, or all together at maturity (cumulative).
  • Rated by a credit rating agency such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings.
  • Secured NCDs are backed by the company’s assets. Unsecured NCDs are not, and are repaid after secured ones if the company fails.

Often confused with

Bank fixed deposits. Bank deposits are insured up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank by DICGC. NCDs are not insured; repayment depends on the company.

13Facts as of October 2026
05 · NCDsBuild

SEBI, for the issue and listing. If the company is an NBFC (a finance company that is not a bank), RBI regulates it too.
Minimum
Usually ₹10,000 when a company offers NCDs to the public (a public issue).
Time commitment
The period of the option (series) you pick, usually 18 months to 10 years.
Money out
Interest as you chose, and your money back at maturity. You can sell earlier on the stock exchange, but the price may be lower and buyers may be few.
Costs
No fee to apply in a public issue. You need a demat account, and brokerage applies if you sell.
Tax in brief
Interest is taxed at your slab rate. If you sell a listed NCD after 12 months, 12.5% on the gain; within 12 months, your slab rate.

  • Is it secured, and what is the asset cover?

  • What if I need my money before maturity?

PMS

Portfolio management services · regulated by SEBI

A SEBI-registered portfolio manager runs a portfolio of shares or bonds just for you. Unlike a mutual fund, the securities sit in your own demat account, so you can see every holding and every trade.

How to recognise it

  • The shares are bought in your name and held in your own demat account.
  • Every PMS reports its returns against a set benchmark for its type of strategy, so managers can be compared.
  • No upfront fees are allowed. Fees are fixed, linked to profits above a set level (the hurdle), or both.

Often confused with

Mutual funds. A shared pool. You own units, not the shares.

AIFs. A pooled fund with a ₹1 crore minimum. It can hold unlisted companies and may lock in your money for years.

AIF

Alternative investment funds · regulated by SEBI

An AIF is a private fund that pools money from a small group of investors. It can invest where most investors cannot: in companies before they list, loans to private companies, commercial real estate and start-ups. Some AIFs also run specialist strategies in listed shares.

How to recognise it

  • Many AIFs give you a share of companies while they are still private, often years before they list.
  • You promise (commit) an amount. The manager asks for it in parts (capital calls) as deals are found.
  • Offered only privately (private placement), to at most 1,000 investors in each scheme.

Often confused with

PMS. Your own account, mostly listed shares, and no lock-in. An AIF pools money and may hold assets that take time to sell.

Regulator
SEBI, under the AIF Regulations, 2012.
Minimum
₹1 crore commitment, paid in parts as the fund invests.
Time commitment
Category I and II: a fixed term, often 4 to 10 years. Category III: open-ended, or a fixed term.
Money out

Costs

Tax in brief
Category I and II: income is mostly taxed in your hands (pass-through). Category III: the fund pays the tax before paying you.

SpecialiseKnow your products · 07 in depth

Private markets

Where the early growth happens

Many Indian companies now stay private for ten years or more before they list on a stock exchange. Some of a company’s growth happens in those private years, before most investors can buy its shares. AIFs let eligible investors take part earlier, with more risk and a longer wait.

The life of a company, before and after it listsIllustration

13.3 years

from founding to listing, on average, for Indian tech companies that listed in 2025.Orios Venture Partners

USD 36 billion

(about ₹3 lakh crore) invested by private equity and venture capital funds in Indian companies in 2025, across about 1,700 deals.Bain & Company and IVCA

87%

of US companies with over USD 100 million in yearly revenue are private, not listed. Private companies are a large part of any economy.S&P Capital IQ data, via Apollo Global Management

What this means for you

At an IPO, early investors often sell part of their stake to the public. To own a share of a company while it is still private, you need to invest before it lists, through an AIF. This means waiting several years. Some companies never list, and some list below their private value.

GIFT City

International investing via GIFT IFSC · regulated by IFSCA

GIFT City in Gujarat is home to India’s International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). Resident Indians can invest there in US dollars, within their yearly LRS limit, through firms regulated by IFSCA.

How to recognise it

  • You invest in US dollars. What you get back depends on the markets and on the rupee–dollar rate.
  • It uses your Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) limit of USD 2,50,000 (over ₹2 crore) per person per financial year. Travel, studies and gifts abroad share it.
  • Your bank collects 20% TCS on money sent abroad to invest above ₹10 lakh a year. You can adjust it against your tax or claim a refund.

Often confused with

International funds in rupees. Sold in India in rupees, but they can stop taking new money when the industry’s overseas limit is reached.

Foreign broker accounts. Your money is held overseas, under that country’s regulator.

Know your productsWords to know

Words to know

Terms used in this guide, in plain words.

Accredited investor. An investor certified as meeting set income or wealth tests. Some products then allow lower minimums.

AMC. Asset management company: the fund house that runs mutual funds and SIFs.

Arbitrage. Buying a share and selling its futures contract at the same time, to earn the small price gap.

Asset cover. How much the assets backing a secured NCD are worth, compared with what is owed.

Benchmark. A market index used to judge how well a manager has done.

Capital call. A request for part of the money you committed to an AIF. Also called a drawdown.

Carried interest. The AIF manager’s share of profits above the hurdle.

Co-payment. The share of each health claim you pay yourself.

Credit rating. An agency’s opinion of how likely a borrower is to pay on time, from AAA to D.

Deductible. The part of a year’s bills that a top-up policy does not pay.

Demat account. An account that holds your shares, bonds and NCDs in electronic form.

Derivatives. Futures and options: contracts whose value moves with a share or an index.

Equity-oriented. A fund or strategy with 65% or more in Indian shares, taxed like an equity fund.

Exit load. A charge for selling mutual fund units within a set period.

Exposure. How much of a fund moves with the market. A SIF can take it below zero.

Hedge. A position that rises when your holdings fall, to cushion the loss.

High-water mark. A rule that a performance fee is paid only on gains above the portfolio’s previous highest value.

Hurdle. The minimum profit investors must receive before the manager shares in profits.

IPO. Initial public offer: when a company first sells shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.

KYC. Know your customer: the identity and address check every investor completes.

Long-short. Owning shares expected to rise, and betting against those expected to fall.

LRS. Liberalised Remittance Scheme: up to USD 2,50,000 abroad per person, per financial year.

LTCG and STCG. Long- and short-term capital gains tax on profit when you sell, redeem or switch. For equity, within 12 months is short-term.

Moratorium. After 5 years of continuous health cover, a claim cannot be refused for a health detail left out, except in fraud.

NAV. Net asset value: the price of one mutual fund unit, worked out every business day.

NBFC. Non-banking financial company: a finance company that is not a bank.

Nominee. The person you name to receive the money from a policy or investment in your absence.

Old tax regime. The older way of filing tax, with deductions such as for premiums. The new regime applies unless you choose the old one.

Pass-through. Income mostly taxed in your hands, not in the fund, as for AIF Category I and II.

Portfolio. All your investments together. Your core portfolio is the main, steady part your goals rely on.

PRIM. A new kind of PMS, from 1 April 2027, that invests only in mutual funds, from ₹25 lakh.

Private equity. Funds that buy stakes in growing private companies.

Private markets. Companies and assets not listed on a stock exchange.

Redeem, switch. Redeem: take your money out of a fund. Switch: move it to another fund or strategy.

REIT, InvIT. Listed trusts that own rental property (REIT) or roads, power lines and similar assets (InvIT).

Risk Band. The risk label for every SIF strategy, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

Riskometer. SEBI’s six-level risk label shown on every mutual fund scheme.

Short position. A holding that gains when a share or index falls.

SIP. Systematic investment plan: a fixed amount invested at regular intervals.

Slab rate. Your income-tax rate, the same rate you pay on income from salary or business.

Sum assured, sum insured. What a life policy pays on a claim; the most a health policy pays in a year.

TCS. Tax collected at source: tax your bank collects when you send large amounts abroad. It is adjusted against your tax.

TER. Total expense ratio: a fund’s yearly running costs, taken from the NAV. SEBI caps its base part.

Venture capital. Money for young, fast-growing private companies, years before they list.

Waiting period. The time after you buy health cover before some illnesses are covered.

How we help you

  • We stay with you when markets fall, so a bad month does not undo a long-term plan.
  • We match each product to a goal, and explain it before you sign.
  • We review everything you hold with us, once a year at least.
  • We handle the paperwork: KYC, nominees, SIPs, switches and redemptions.
  • We give you the papers your tax consultant needs.
  • If something happens to you, we help your family with claims and transfers.

How we are paid

We receive commission from the providers of the products we distribute. It pays for this service, for as long as you invest with us.

Standard warnings

Mutual Fund investments are subject to market risks, read all scheme related documents carefully.

Investments in Specialized Investment Fund involves relatively higher risk including potential loss of capital, liquidity risk and market volatility. Please read all investment strategy related documents carefully before making the investment decision.

Investments in debt securities/municipal debt securities/securitised debt instruments are subject to risks including delay and/or default in payment. Read all the offer related documents carefully.

For more details on risk factors, terms and conditions please read sales brochure carefully before concluding a sale. (Insurance)

Investments in securities are subject to market risks. Read the disclosure document carefully before investing. (PMS)

AIFs are offered only by private placement to eligible investors.

If you have a complaint

Contact us first at support@raminvestments.in or on the numbers above.
